title: Stoicism in Thirty Days
blurb: A month with the two Stoics who wrote to be used rather than admired: Epictetus, a former slave who taught, and Marcus Aurelius, an emperor who took notes. Alternating books, roughly twenty minutes a day. Read a little and stop; that is how these were meant to work.

steps.label: Days 1–5 · What is up to us
steps.blurb: Epictetus opens with the only distinction that matters to him: some things are in our power and some are not. Everything else follows from it.

steps.label: Days 6–8 · Begin the morning
steps.blurb: Marcus rehearses the day's irritations before they arrive. Notice that he is talking to himself, not to you.

steps.label: Days 9–13 · Training
steps.blurb: How to practice when nothing has gone wrong yet, so that you have something to draw on when it does.

steps.label: Days 14–16 · The retreat within
steps.blurb: The famous passage about retiring into yourself, and the running argument about death that Marcus never finishes.

steps.label: Days 17–21 · On freedom
steps.blurb: Epictetus on what a free person actually is, written by someone who had been owned.

steps.label: Days 22–24 · On other people
steps.blurb: The books where Marcus is hardest on himself about being hard on others.

steps.label: Days 25–28 · Living it
steps.blurb: The last book, and the most practical: what the doctrine looks like on an ordinary afternoon.

steps.label: Days 29–30 · Leaving
steps.blurb: The final book, written near the end of his life on campaign. Read it slowly.
